walkthroughs.body_html: Tipping points are thresholds where a small change pushes a system into a new state. Examples include the AMOC slowdown, Amazon dieback, West Antarctic ice sheet collapse and permafrost thaw releasing methane. Once crossed, these changes are often irreversible on human timescales and can trigger cascading effects globally.

Signed in 2015, the Paris Agreement commits nearly all countries to keep global warming well below 2 C and pursue 1.5 C. Countries set Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and review them every five years. Reaching 1.5 C requires roughly halving emissions by 2030 and net zero by around 2050.

Positive feedbacks amplify warming. Melting Arctic sea ice exposes dark ocean which absorbs more heat (ice-albedo feedback). Thawing permafrost releases methane, intensifying warming. Drying forests burn more, adding CO2. Negative feedbacks like increased plant growth offer limited cooling and may saturate.
